summary: Silicon spin qubits fabricated in industrial and academic facilities exhibit remarkably consistent power-law degradation of gate fidelity with temperature, with a characteristic crossover near 1 K above which performance degrades rapidly. A system-level power model combining cryogenic cooling requirements with quantum error correction overhead predicts a finite optimal operating temperature of 0.5–1.5 K that balances refrigeration cost against the physical-qubit overhead needed to maintain logical performance.
motivation: Utility-scale silicon quantum computers will generate thermal loads exceeding dilution-refrigerator cooling power at millikelvin temperatures, yet cooling power increases dramatically with operating temperature while qubit fidelity degrades. Understanding the trade-off between cryogenic cooling requirements and error-correction overhead is essential for identifying the commercially viable operating point.
method: Gate set tomography characterizes the temperature dependence of single- and two-qubit gate fidelities, relaxation times, and coherence times across six silicon MOS double-quantum-dot devices (three from imec's 300 mm industrial process with 400 ppm residual $^{29}$Si, three from academic facilities with 50–800 ppm $^{29}$Si). Measured infidelities are fit to power-law forms $\mathcal{M} = \kappa[1 + (T/T_X)^n]$ and combined with surface-code error-correction scaling and generalized Carnot refrigerator modeling to compute total system power as a function of temperature.
result: Device A achieves $>99.9\%$ SPAM and single-qubit fidelity, $>99\%$ two-qubit fidelity up to 0.5–0.7 K; above 1 K, fidelities degrade rapidly due to dephasing. The power model shows a well-defined optimum at 0.5–1.5 K for realistic silicon architectures with 500 logical qubits, demonstrating that minimizing total power does not require millikelvin operation and that the crossover temperature $T_X = 0.5$–1 K strongly influences the optimal point.
